The study guide lists twelve course lessons but no topics or weights. This pack groups lessons 2 to 11 into eight objectives, weighted by how many course lessons each covers, and splits each into two or three topics, 19 in all. Every topic has a lesson in the same shape: the idea, a worked example, the exam trap, a self-check, more detail, a worked case, an exercise with its solution, the facts to learn, and a note on what was verified. Short mocks draw 10 questions at random. The six full papers, A to F, each have 20 fixed single-select questions weighted like the course. lessons.title: 1.1 · Built-in quality: principles connected to practices
lessons.summary: Why quality sets the pace, the XP practices, the definition of done and technical debt.

blocks.text:
Built-In Quality is a set of practices that help Agile teams meet quality standards while they create customer value. SAFe's argument is economic: quality determines how fast a team can deliver. A defect found a minute after it is written costs a minute. The same defect found in production costs an incident, a fix, a retest and a redeployment.

So the team shifts learning left, which means finding problems sooner. The listed benefits are higher customer satisfaction, improved velocity and delivery predictability, better system performance, and an improved ability to innovate, scale and meet compliance requirements.
blocks.title: Quality sets the pace

blocks.text:
Agile software engineering takes most of its technical practices from Extreme Programming. Pair programming reviews code as it is written and spreads knowledge. Collective ownership lets anyone improve any code, supported by tests and standards. Continuous integration merges and verifies changes frequently. Test-driven development writes the test first. Refactoring improves structure without changing behaviour. Simple design builds what is needed now.

Two definitions matter. The definition of done is the requirements for completeness of a work product. Technical debt is the future cost of rework created by shortcuts taken now.
blocks.title: Principles connected to practices

rows: Anyone may improve any code, backed by tests
Code that reads as if one person wrote it
Small changes merged and verified many times a day
Tests that define and protect behaviour
Design kept simple as the code grows
Quality that does not collapse under overtime
blocks.title: XP practices that build quality in

blocks.text: One developer at Osric Bank understands the billing module, and every billing story waits for her. The team starts pairing on billing stories and agrees that anyone may change the module once the tests pass. Within two iterations four people can work there, the queue is gone, and the unit tests written while pairing catch a rounding defect before it leaves the team.
blocks.title: Worked example · Osric Bank

blocks.text: "Go faster by leaving tests until later" is always the wrong answer: quality determines how fast a team can go. A story that passes its acceptance tests but has no unit tests and unreviewed code is not done.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What is technical debt? The future cost of rework caused by choosing an easy solution now; it makes every later change slower and riskier until repaid.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: A team inherits a codebase with no tests. Rather than stopping delivery for a rewrite, it adds characterization and unit tests around each area it changes, story by story, and reserves capacity each iteration for refactoring. Defects fall where the team works most.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Strengthen this definition of done: "code complete".
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: For example: unit and acceptance tests automated and passing, code reviewed or paired, merged to the main branch and built by the pipeline, and no known defects introduced. That makes "done" mean releasable.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Built-in quality: practices that help work meet quality standards throughout. Benefits include velocity and predictability. Shift learning left. XP practices. Definition of done. Technical debt and refactoring capacity. T-shaped skills and collective ownership.

lessons.title: 1.2 · Accelerating flow
lessons.summary: Small batches, WIP limits, trunk-based development, the pipeline, deployment versus release, and recovery.

blocks.text: Value flows when work moves in small batches with fast feedback. Large batches delay feedback and make each defect more expensive. A feature carries a benefit hypothesis, the proposed measurable benefit. It is validated by releasing something small and measuring what real users do. Passing tests shows the feature was built as specified. Only evidence shows it was worth building.
blocks.title: Accelerating flow

rows: Shorter waits and less context switching
No long-lived branches or painful merges
Feedback in seconds before a commit
Deploy now, release when the business chooses
Lower release risk and quick rollback
blocks.title: Practices that accelerate flow

blocks.text: A team's feature branches live for weeks and merges take days. It moves to trunk-based development: small changes merged to main at least daily, unfinished work hidden behind toggles, and a pipeline that builds, tests and deploys each change. Lead time for changes falls from weeks to days.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: A separate DevOps team, a code freeze before each release, or a big release once a year are the classic wrong answers. Release is a business decision separate from deployment, and the main branch should always be releasable.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: New code is deployed but hidden until marketing is ready. Which technique allows this? A feature toggle.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: SAFe's pipeline has four aspects: Continuous Exploration, Continuous Integration, Continuous Deployment and Release on Demand. For an engineer, Continuous Integration means develop, build, test end to end and stage; Continuous Deployment moves validated changes to production, where they are verified and monitored. CALMR, culture, automation, Lean flow, measurement and recovery, describes the DevOps approach behind it. Recovery means designing for automated rollback or fix-forward.
blocks.title: The Continuous Delivery Pipeline

blocks.text: Stories wait days for a separate test team. The team moves testers into the story from the start, automates acceptance checks as the code is written, and limits work in progress. The queue disappears, and so does the end-of-iteration crunch.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Name the technique: (a) 5% of users get the new version first; (b) two production environments with traffic switched between them; (c) environments built from version-controlled scripts.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Canary release. (b) Blue-green deployment. (c) Infrastructure as code.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Small batches and WIP limits. Trunk-based development. Deployment pipeline. Lead time for changes. Deployment versus release; toggles. Canary and blue-green. CALMR. Value stream maps show where work waits.

lessons.title: 2.1 · Intentional architecture, emergent design and the runway
lessons.summary: Balancing emergent and intentional design, the System Architect, the runway, enablers and spikes.

blocks.text:
Agile Architecture is a set of values, practices and collaborations that support the active, evolutionary design and architecture of a system. It avoids big design up front. It supports design simplicity, a balance of intentional and emergent design, and designing for testability, deployability and releasability.

Emergent design means each team defines what the next increment needs. At scale that is not enough: without shared direction, teams produce one-off solutions that do not fit together. Intentional architecture adds some planning and cross-team coordination. The Architectural Runway, built by enablers, is the result both rely on.

Systems thinking is the habit of looking at the whole. Optimising one service can slow the transaction the customer cares about.
blocks.title: Architecture in an Agile setting

blocks.text: Next PI's features need an event-streaming platform that does not exist. The train plans architectural enabler work ahead of those features, so the runway is in place when the features start. Without it, each feature would carry hidden foundation work and slow down.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Neither big design up front nor pure emergence is SAFe's answer; it is emergent design within intentional architecture. Teams do not choose system-wide technology alone, and architects do not veto from a distance; they decide together.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A team cannot estimate a story because nobody knows how a new library behaves. What should it plan? A spike: a short, time-boxed exploration to gain the knowledge needed.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

rows: Knowledge, through research, prototypes and spikes
The technical runway of the solution
blocks.title: Four kinds of enabler

blocks.text: Classify: (a) building automated test environments; (b) a two-day investigation of a queueing library; (c) logging changes required by an audit.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Infrastructure enabler. (b) Exploration enabler, a spike. (c) Compliance enabler.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Agile architecture: values, practices and collaborations that support active, evolutionary design. Emergent design plus intentional architecture. The System Architect guides shared design. Set-based design keeps options open. Runway is extended by enablers, made visible in the backlog.

lessons.title: 2.2 · Designing for testability and deployability
lessons.summary: Seams, dependency injection, controllable time, observability and releasable designs.

blocks.text:
Set-Based Design keeps design options open and converges on evidence. A spike is an enabler story used to gain knowledge that reduces risk or makes an estimate reliable.

Designing for testability mostly means controlling dependencies. Code that creates its own database connection can only be tested with a database. Code that receives a collaborator through an interface can be tested with a substitute.
blocks.title: Options, spikes and testability
C# · A seam for testing

blocks.text: A team at Ulverston Energy cannot estimate a metering story because nobody knows whether a new time-series library copes with the load. It plans a two-day spike, runs a load test, and learns the library is fast enough only with batching. The story is then estimated with that design, and an architectural enabler adds a shared batching component to the runway for the other teams.
blocks.title: Worked example · Ulverston Energy

blocks.text: Retries, test ordering and "run the tests only in office hours" hide testability flaws instead of fixing them. The fix is a design change: inject the dependency, whether a repository, a clock or a gateway.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A C# class calls DateTime.Now, so tests fail around midnight. What improves testability? Inject a clock abstraction, such as TimeProvider in .NET 8 and later, that tests can control.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution
C# · Controllable time

blocks.text: Deployability means parts of the system can be deployed small, safely and often; releasability means the business can choose when customers see them, for example through feature toggles. Observability, through logs, metrics and traces that are collected and used, lets teams understand the system in production. These qualities are designed in, like testability, not added at the end.
blocks.title: Designing for operation

blocks.text: A service logs only to a local file nobody reads, and every release changes a schema shared by all teams. Name two qualities to improve.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Observability: send logs, metrics and traces to a shared platform with alerts. Deployability: decouple the schema so teams can deploy independently, for example with versioned contracts.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Design for testability, deployability and releasability. Inject dependencies through interfaces. Control time and other non-determinism. Observability. Architects work with teams, not only through documents.

lessons.title: 3.1 · Test-first thinking and the Agile testing matrix
lessons.summary: Test-first as a way of thinking, the four quadrants, and exploratory testing.

blocks.text: Agile testing develops and tests in small increments, and often writes the test before the code, story or feature. Quality is built in from the start, the whole team shares responsibility for it, and tests are automated wherever possible. Shifting testing left means the test exists when the work begins, so a defect is found close to the moment it is introduced.
blocks.title: Test-first as a way of thinking

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge of the testing quadrants; the SAFe article is behind a login.
rows: Functional and story acceptance tests, often automated with BDD
Exploratory, usability and user acceptance testing, largely manual
Unit and component tests, automated with TDD
Performance, security and other system quality tests
blocks.title: The Agile testing matrix

blocks.text: Before coding a discount rule, a developer and a tester write three examples with inputs and expected results. Writing them exposes a question nobody had asked: does the discount apply before or after tax? The Product Owner answers, and the examples become the first tests.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: The quadrants mix two axes: business-facing or technology-facing, and guiding development or critiquing the product. Unit tests guide from the technology side; functional tests guide from the business side; exploratory tests critique from the business side; performance and security tests critique from the technology side.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Which quadrant holds exploratory and usability testing? Business-facing tests that critique the product.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: A team writes tests after each story and keeps finding it misunderstood the requirement. It starts agreeing examples before development, in refinement, so 'working' is defined up front and rework drops.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Place in quadrants: (a) a load test; (b) an xUnit test of a tax calculator; (c) a Gherkin scenario agreed with the PO; (d) a tester exploring a new screen.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Technology-facing, critique. (b) Technology-facing, guide. (c) Business-facing, guide. (d) Business-facing, critique.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Test-first: agree how you will know something works before building it. Agile testing matrix: four quadrants on two axes. Exploratory testing finds what scripts miss. Shift testing left.

lessons.title: 3.2 · The test pyramid, automation and NFR testing
lessons.summary: Balancing the test portfolio, contract tests, and testing nonfunctional requirements continuously.

blocks.text:
Nonfunctional requirements are system qualities such as performance, scalability, security, usability and maintainability. They guide design and often act as constraints across the backlogs. They are revisited as part of the definition of done for each iteration, planning interval or release, which in practice means an automated check.

A healthy test portfolio is shaped like a pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer component and integration tests, and a small number of slow end-to-end tests. Writing tests first tends to produce that shape. Quality is then checked at each stage of the pipeline, not at one late gate.
blocks.title: NFRs and the pyramid

blocks.text: The regression suite at Varnham Retail is four hours of browser tests. Developers run it once a day and ignore intermittent failures. The team moves the price and stock rules into unit tests that run in seconds, keeps a dozen browser tests for the main journeys, and adds a response-time check to the pipeline. Feedback on a change drops from a day to ten minutes.
blocks.title: Worked example · Varnham Retail

blocks.text: The inverted pyramid, many UI tests and few unit tests, is a common distractor phrased as "realistic". Running a slow suite less often makes feedback later; moving checks down the pyramid is the fix.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: How should a team test that an API responds within 200 ms at peak load? With an automated performance test in the pipeline, run regularly.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

rows: xUnit tests of domain and service classes
API and contract tests between services
A few key journeys through the UI
Performance, security and reliability checks in the pipeline
blocks.title: A balanced portfolio for a C# web API

blocks.text: A suite takes three hours, so developers stop running it. Name two changes.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Move business-rule checks from UI tests down to unit and service tests, and use contract tests instead of full end-to-end runs between services. Keep a few UI journeys.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Many unit tests, fewer service tests, few UI tests. UI tests are slow and brittle. Contract tests let services be tested independently. NFRs are tested continuously, like functional behaviour.

lessons.title: 4.1 · Writing stories: the 3Cs, INVEST and acceptance criteria
lessons.summary: What a story is, the user-voice format, INVEST, enabler stories and testable acceptance criteria.

blocks.text:
A story is a short description of a small piece of desired functionality, written from the user's perspective. It is a vertical slice of system behaviour that a team can finish within one iteration, usually in a few days. User stories describe value to an end user. Enabler stories describe exploration, architecture, infrastructure and compliance work. The team writes and estimates stories together.

Details are deferred until the story is about to be built. Acceptance criteria then make it specific: they give the information needed to confirm the story is implemented correctly. Do not confuse them with the definition of done, which applies to every story.
blocks.title: What a story is

rows: Can be built in any order
Delivers value to a user or the business
The team understands it well enough to size
blocks.title: INVEST

blocks.text:
Feature: Pay for a booking

  Scenario: Pay the full amount by card
    Given a booking with a balance of 120.00
    When the customer pays 120.00 by card
    Then the booking is marked as paid
    And a receipt is sent to the customer

  Scenario: Card is declined
    Given a booking with a balance of 120.00
    When the card payment is declined
    Then the booking remains unpaid
    And the customer is asked for another payment method
blocks.title: Gherkin · Acceptance criteria as examples

blocks.text: "The system shall" statements and tasks such as "build the database tables" are not user stories. Acceptance criteria must be checkable: "quick and easy" is not; "a reset link expires 30 minutes after it is sent" is.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What are the 3Cs? Card, conversation and confirmation.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Rewrite as a user story: "Add saved cards to the payment table".
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: "As a returning shopper, I want to save my card so that I can pay faster next time," with criteria such as "a saved card can be chosen at checkout" and "only the last four digits are shown".
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Story: a short description of a small piece of value, sized for an iteration. User-voice format: who, what, why. 3Cs. INVEST. Enabler stories for technical work. Acceptance criteria as testable examples.

lessons.title: 4.2 · Splitting stories and story mapping
lessons.summary: Vertical slices, the main splitting patterns, story maps and spikes.

blocks.text:
A story that is too large is split so that each part still delivers behaviour someone can see and accept. Useful splits follow workflow steps, business rules, data variations or the simple case before the complex one. Splits by layer, such as interface then database, or by activity, such as code then test, give pieces that cannot be accepted alone.

Splitting also shrinks the Minimum Marketable Feature, the smallest set of functionality worth releasing, which shortens time to value and to feedback.

A story map arranges user activities from left to right and stories beneath them by priority. It shows gaps in the journey and helps choose a thin first slice. While discovering details, the team also writes down its assumptions and risks, and plans a spike where one of them is large.
blocks.title: Splitting

rows: Search, then choose seats, then pay
Create and view first, edit and delete later
Explore the unknown, then estimate the rest
blocks.title: Common splitting patterns

blocks.text: The story 'pay for a booking' at Zennor Travel is estimated at three iterations. The team splits it by business rule: card payment in full, then vouchers, then part payment. The first slice goes through the interface, the service and the database for one rule, and it is demonstrated at the end of the iteration. The earlier idea, building the payment tables first, would have produced nothing to show.
blocks.title: Worked example · Zennor Travel

blocks.text: Splitting by layer (UI, logic, database) or by activity (coding, testing) produces pieces no user can use. Every slice should be vertical and deliver value end to end.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: How does a team choose a first release on a story map? It draws a line across the map under the essential stories, so users can complete the whole journey.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Split "customers can manage their addresses".
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: For example, by operations: add an address, then edit it, then delete it, then set a default. Each slice is usable and testable on its own.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Vertical slices. Splitting patterns. Story map: backbone of user activities in order, stories beneath, release lines across. Minimum marketable feature. Spikes when uncertainty blocks estimation.
blocks.title: Details to know

blocks.text:
Generic answer: a story is a small requirement document. SAFe answer: it is a short description, with details discovered in conversation and captured as acceptance criteria.

Wrong size test: a story fits in an iteration; a feature fits in a planning interval.

Wrong split: by layer or by task.

Wrong owner: the product owner defines and accepts stories, and the team writes and estimates them together. A manager does not assign estimates.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

lessons.title: 5.1 · Writing good scenarios in Gherkin
lessons.summary: Given, When, Then; declarative steps; Scenario Outline and Background; one behaviour per scenario.

blocks.text:
Given sets the context. When states the action or event. Then states the outcome that should be observed. A good scenario uses domain terms the business recognises and says nothing about buttons, colours or tables.

Business rules and calculations are best tested below the user interface, directly against the domain logic. Keep a small number of interface tests for the screens themselves. Where a scenario depends on something slow, costly or unavailable, replace it with a test double.
blocks.title: Good scenarios

rows: Names the capability and its value
Given steps every scenario in the file shares
Continue the previous kind of step
Run one scenario with rows of data
blocks.title: Gherkin keywords

blocks.text: "When the user clicks the blue Submit button in the footer" describes the interface, and breaks when the button moves. "When the customer submits the order" describes behaviour and survives a redesign. The step definition, not the scenario, knows about buttons.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Then steps that check database rows or method calls test the implementation. A scenario with many When and Then steps tests too much; split it by behaviour.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What is a Scenario Outline for? Running one scenario with several rows of example data from an Examples table.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Improve: "Given the system has some data. When the user clicks around. Then everything works."
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: For example: "Given a customer with 3 unpaid invoices. When the customer pays the oldest invoice. Then 2 invoices remain unpaid." Concrete context, one action, one checkable outcome.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Given, When, Then. Declarative over imperative. One behaviour per scenario. Concrete values. Scenario Outline and Examples. Background for shared context.

lessons.title: 5.2 · BDD in practice: collaboration and automation
lessons.summary: Three amigos, specification by example, living documentation and automating below the interface.

blocks.text:
Behavior-Driven Development is a test-first Agile testing practice. It defines, and possibly automates, tests before or as part of specifying behaviour. Its first purpose is shared understanding between the business and the team, which guides development, reduces rework and increases flow.

Three perspectives are needed, known as the triad: customer-centric, development-centric and test-centric. Together they agree concrete examples of how the system should behave. The examples become business-facing scenarios that describe behaviour from the user's point of view without describing the implementation. Automated, they keep the behaviour correct as the system changes and show which existing behaviour a new requirement touches.
blocks.title: What BDD is for

blocks.text:
Scenario Outline: Loyalty discount
  Given a customer with <years> years of membership
  When they check out a basket worth <total>
  Then the discount is <discount>

  Examples:
    | years | total  | discount |
    | 0     | 100.00 | 0.00     |
    | 3     | 100.00 | 5.00     |
    | 10    | 100.00 | 10.00    |

// Step definitions call the domain object, not the browser.
[When(@"they check out a basket worth (.*)")]
public void WhenTheyCheckOut(decimal total) =>
    _discount = _calculator.DiscountFor(_customer, total);

[Then(@"the discount is (.*)")]
public void ThenTheDiscountIs(decimal expected) =>
    Assert.Equal(expected, _discount);
blocks.title: Gherkin and C# · A rule tested below the interface

blocks.text: A fare rule at Corbin Travel depends on a partner service that is slow and charges per call. The product owner, a developer and a tester agree five examples in twenty minutes and find two cases nobody had considered. The scenarios run against the fare calculator with a test double in place of the partner, so the whole set runs in under a second on every commit.
blocks.title: Worked example · Corbin Travel

blocks.text: BDD is not a QA testing tool; it is a collaboration practice that produces tests. The conversation happens before development. Automating every scenario through the browser makes the suite slow and fragile.

lessons.title: 6.1 · Static models: domain, class and CRC
lessons.summary: Why model, domain models, class diagrams and CRC cards, and how much to model.

blocks.text:
A model is a cheap way to explore and communicate a design. SAFe treats modelling as a Lean tool: it gives early feedback on requirements and design before the cost of change rises. Agile modelling is just enough to learn and to agree, drawn on a whiteboard as often as in a tool.

A domain model describes the entities of the problem domain and the relationships between them. It gives the business and the teams a common language, and the same words then appear in stories, scenarios and code.
blocks.title: Why model at all

blocks.text: Written from the author's knowledge of common modelling practice.
rows: Class diagram, component diagram, domain model
Sequence diagram, state diagram, activity diagram
blocks.title: Static and dynamic models

blocks.text:
Class-Responsibility-Collaboration is a lightweight technique. Each index card names one class, lists what it is responsible for, and lists the classes it collaborates with. The team then walks through a scenario, passing control from card to card.

The cards make design problems physical. A card with too many responsibilities is a class with low cohesion. A card that collaborates with everything is a class with high coupling.
blocks.title: CRC cards

blocks.text: During a CRC session, one card collects fifteen responsibilities and twelve collaborators. The team reads that as low cohesion and high coupling, splits the card into three classes with clear purposes, and moves responsibilities so that each card has a few collaborators.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: SAFe's ASE course treats modelling as a Lean tool: just enough to communicate and explore. Complete models before coding, or models of every class kept up to date by hand, are the wrong answer.

blocks.text: A new developer needs to understand how Book, Member and Loan relate in a library system. Which model would you sketch?

blocks.text: A domain model showing the three concepts and their relationships: a Member has Loans; each Loan is of one Book.

blocks.text: Models explore and communicate design. Domain model: business concepts and relationships. Class diagram: classes, members, relationships. CRC: class, responsibilities, collaborators. Just enough modelling.

blocks.text: A team at Hadleigh Pay argues about what can happen to an order after payment fails. A state diagram on the whiteboard settles it in ten minutes: created, paid, failed, retried, cancelled, with the event that causes each move. Two missing transitions become stories. A CRC walk-through of 'retry payment' then shows the Order card doing work that belongs on a new PaymentAttempt card.

blocks.text: A sequence diagram follows an interaction across several objects; a state diagram follows one object's life. A diagram with one object calling eight others is not ideal design; it signals centralised control.

blocks.text: An invoice can be Draft, Sent, Paid or Cancelled, and some transitions are not allowed. Which model captures this? A state diagram.

blocks.text: Static models show what exists; dynamic models show how it works together. Chatty interactions, a god object orchestrating everything, or a missing state such as "refund pending" show up only when behaviour is drawn. Throwaway whiteboard sketches that help a team decide are good practice; keep a model only if it keeps helping.

blocks.text: Which model would you sketch to see the calls between the order, payment and stock services during checkout?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: A sequence diagram, with the three services across the top and the messages in time order.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Sequence: messages over time. State: one object's states and events, with guards. Activity: process steps and decisions. Dynamic models complement static ones. Simple sketches shared early.

Traditional answer: complete the models before coding. SAFe answer: model just enough to learn, and keep learning.

Wrong diagram: a class diagram for a question about behaviour over time. Use a sequence or state diagram.

lessons.title: 7.1 · Code quality: cohesion, coupling, duplication and smells
lessons.summary: The qualities of good code, the common smells and the refactorings that fix them.

blocks.text:
Cohesion is how closely the parts of a module relate to one purpose. Coupling is how much one module depends on others. Code is easiest to change with high cohesion and loose coupling. Other qualities follow from these: no duplication, so one piece of knowledge lives in one place; encapsulation, so details can change without affecting callers; readability; and testability.

Collective ownership means anyone on the team may improve any code. It is safe when automated tests catch regressions and shared coding standards keep the code familiar.
blocks.title: Code qualities

rows: Uses another class's data more than its own
Strings and decimals for domain ideas
blocks.title: Common code smells

blocks.text: A tax change at Ingram Retail needs edits in nine classes, and one is missed. The cause is duplication: each class computes tax itself. The team extracts a TaxPolicy behind an interface, has the nine classes ask it, and covers it with unit tests. The next tax change is one edit and one test.

blocks.text: Comments are not a fix for unclear code, and splitting a long method by position keeps the tangle. Cohesion is about one purpose; coupling is about dependence on others: distractors swap them.

blocks.text: Which combination makes code easiest to change? High cohesion and loose coupling.

blocks.text: Cohesion, coupling, DRY, intention-revealing names. Smells: long method, duplication, feature envy, shotgun surgery, primitive obsession, long parameter list, dead code. Cyclomatic complexity. Reviews and pairing spread standards.

blocks.text: An InvoiceService calculates totals and formats PDF output. The team moves PDF rendering into its own class, so pricing changes and layout changes no longer touch the same file. That is the single responsibility principle.

blocks.text: DRY keeps each piece of knowledge in one place. YAGNI, you aren't gonna need it, warns against speculative features and flexibility. The Law of Demeter advises talking only to immediate collaborators, avoiding chains such as order.Customer.Address.City. Simple design means the least structure that passes the tests and expresses intent.

blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: YAGNI. Keep the design simple and easy to extend, and add the plugin system when a real need appears.

lessons.title: 7.3 · Interfaces and design patterns
lessons.summary: Programming to interfaces and the patterns most likely to appear: Strategy, Adapter, Decorator, Observer and others.

blocks.text:
Interface-oriented design defines the contract a collaborator must meet and lets implementations vary behind it. When several designs are plausible, keep the options open and decide on evidence.

Design patterns are named solutions to recurring problems. Strategy puts interchangeable algorithms behind one interface. Adapter converts an interface you were given into the one you need. Factory hides how objects are created. Use a pattern when the problem it solves is present. Simple design means not adding it in advance.
blocks.title: Design options, interfaces and patterns
C# · From conditionals to Strategy

rows: Swapping algorithms at run time behind one interface
Making an incompatible interface fit the one clients expect
A simple entry point to a complex subsystem
Adding behaviour, such as logging or caching, by wrapping
Constructing complex objects step by step
Requests as objects, for queues and undo
A fixed algorithm with overridable steps
blocks.title: Patterns to recognise

blocks.text: Adding patterns 'in case they are needed' is speculative complexity. Static singletons hide global dependencies that tests cannot replace; a singleton lifetime in the DI container is the testable alternative.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A team must add logging and caching around a repository without changing it. Which pattern? Decorator.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: A supplier library exposes an interface that does not match the team's own. Which pattern bridges them?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Adapter: a class that implements the team's interface and translates calls to the supplier library.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Program to an interface. Patterns are named solutions to recurring problems; use them when the problem is present. Recognise Strategy, Adapter, Facade, Decorator, Observer, Factory Method, Builder, Command and Template Method. Interfaces let teams work in parallel against a contract.
blocks.title: Details to know

blocks.text:
Generic answer: each component has an owner who approves changes. SAFe and XP answer: collective ownership, made safe by tests and standards.

Wrong principle: empty methods forced by a large interface point to interface segregation, not Liskov. Type checks before calling a subtype point to Liskov.

Wrong instinct: adding patterns for needs that may come. Build for the current need and refactor.

Interface-oriented design is about contracts between components, not about screens.

lessons.title: 8.1 · The TDD cycle
lessons.summary: Red, green, refactor in small steps, good test names and Arrange-Act-Assert.

blocks.text:
Test-Driven Development is a philosophy and practice of building and running tests before implementing the code or component. The cycle has three steps. Red: write a small test for the next behaviour and watch it fail, which proves the test can detect what is missing. Green: write the simplest code that passes. Refactor: improve the design with all tests passing.

The result is code that is tested by construction and shaped by how it is used. Unit tests should be fast and isolated, so dependencies such as a database or a gateway are replaced by test doubles. A stub returns prepared answers. A mock or spy lets the test check how a collaborator was called.
blocks.title: Test-driven development
C# and xUnit · One turn of the cycle

blocks.text: After green comes refactor, not the next feature. Watching a new test fail first proves it can detect the missing behaviour. Big steps defeat the purpose: a failure should point straight at the last small change.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What are the three steps of TDD? Red: a failing test. Green: the simplest code that passes. Refactor: improve the design with all tests green.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Name tests for behaviour and condition, such as Total_IncludesTax_WhenCustomerIsDomestic, so a failure explains itself. Structure each test as Arrange, Act, Assert. Keep tests fast, isolated and repeatable, checking one behaviour each, so they can run on every change and any failure is meaningful.
blocks.title: Writing good unit tests

blocks.text: Write the first failing test for a rule: orders over 50 ship free.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: For example, an xUnit [Fact] named Orders_over_fifty_ship_free that arranges a Shipping object with a stub carrier, acts by calling Rate with an order total of 60, and asserts that the result is 0. It fails until Rate exists and applies the rule.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: TDD: write a test, see it fail, make it pass simply, refactor. Small steps. Behaviour-revealing names. Arrange-Act-Assert. Fast, isolated, repeatable tests.
blocks.title: Details to know

blocks.text: A unit test calls a real payment gateway and fails when the network is slow. Replacing the gateway with a stub that returns a fixed approval makes the test fast and deterministic; a separate contract or integration test covers the real gateway.

blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Stub, mock, spy, fake, dummy. Doubles keep unit tests fast and isolated. Over-mocking makes tests brittle. Mock at boundaries; check outcomes elsewhere.

lessons.title: 8.3 · Refactoring safely
lessons.summary: Refactoring under green tests, characterization tests for legacy code, enabler stories and tool-assisted changes.

blocks.text:
Refactoring improves the internal structure or operation of code or a component without changing its external behaviour. It extends the useful life of software and is what makes emergent design possible.

Small refactorings are part of every story. A larger one is planned as an enabler story: estimable, verifiable, valuable and accepted by the product owner, and it needs capacity.

When new behaviour is needed in tangled code, separate the two kinds of change. First refactor under passing tests to make the change easy. Then add the behaviour test-first.
blocks.title: Refactoring

blocks.text: A fee calculation at Tolland Bank lives in a 400-line method. A new fee type is needed. The pair first writes characterisation tests that pin down current behaviour, then extracts each fee into its own small class with the tests green throughout. Only then do they write a failing test for the new fee and add a class to pass it. The extraction is visible on the board as an enabler story.
blocks.title: Worked example · Tolland Bank

blocks.text: Refactoring changes structure, never behaviour, and it is not a rewrite. In legacy code without tests, characterization tests come first. Large refactorings are planned visibly as enabler stories, not hidden in feature estimates.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Why keep refactoring and adding behaviour as separate steps? Each step stays small and verifiable, so any failure's cause is obvious.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: The boy scout rule, leaving code a little cleaner than you found it, keeps debt from growing. IDE refactorings such as rename, extract method and introduce parameter object understand the code's structure, so they are safer than text replacement. Replacing magic numbers with named constants documents intent and keeps each value in one place.
blocks.title: Everyday refactoring

blocks.text: New behaviour is needed in a tangled, untested class. Put these in order: add the new behaviour test-first; add characterization tests; refactor under the tests.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Add characterization tests, refactor under them, then add the new behaviour test-first.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Refactoring improves structure without changing behaviour. Characterization tests for legacy code. Separate refactoring from new behaviour. Boy scout rule. Tool-assisted refactoring. Large refactorings as enabler stories.
blocks.title: Details to know

blocks.text:
Generic answer: write the code, then the tests. SAFe answer: the test comes first.

Wrong step: refactoring while a test is red, or writing the full implementation at green.

Hidden work: spreading a large refactoring across other stories. SAFe makes it an enabler story.

Refactoring versus rewriting: a refactoring keeps behaviour the same. Adding a feature is a different step.

questions.prompt: What is Built-In Quality in SAFe?

questions.explanation: Built-In Quality is a set of practices that let Agile teams meet quality standards while they create customer value. Quality and speed trade off, so pick one each interval

questions.prompt: What is a story in SAFe?

questions.prompt: A C# method is 300 lines long and does validation, pricing and emailing. What should a developer do?

options.text: Add comments above each section to explain it
Extract one method or class per responsibility
Leave it, since it works and has tests
Split it into three 100-line methods by position

questions.explanation: Extracting each responsibility into its own well-named method or class improves cohesion and testability. Splitting by position keeps the tangle, and comments do not make the code easier to change. Topic 7.1, lesson “7.1 · Code quality: cohesion, coupling, duplication and smells”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is primitive obsession?

options.text: Writing code in an older language for speed
Preferring primitive loops over LINQ in C#
Basic types where a small domain type fits
Refusing to use any third-party libraries

questions.explanation: Passing strings and decimals for things like email addresses and money spreads validation everywhere. Small types such as Email or Money keep the rules in one place. Topic 7.1, lesson “7.1 · Code quality: cohesion, coupling, duplication and smells”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A method takes seven parameters, five of which always travel together. Which refactoring helps?

options.text: Add two more optional parameters
Introduce a parameter object
Make all the parameters static
Convert the method to a property

questions.explanation: Grouping parameters that always travel together into one object, such as a record in C#, shortens the signature and names the concept they form. Adding parameters or making them static does neither. Topic 7.1, lesson “7.1 · Code quality: cohesion, coupling, duplication and smells”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why is dead code harmful even though it never runs?

options.text: It breaks the unit tests that cover it
It misleads readers and costs upkeep
It causes compiler errors in later releases
It slows the program on every request

questions.explanation: Unused code still has to be read, understood and kept compiling, and readers may think it matters. Version control keeps the history, so it can be deleted safely. Topic 7.1, lesson “7.1 · Code quality: cohesion, coupling, duplication and smells”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which metric best signals a class that is hard to test and change?

options.text: A long, descriptive class name
High cyclomatic complexity
A large number of comments
Very few lines of code

questions.explanation: Cyclomatic complexity counts independent paths through code; many paths need many tests and make changes risky. Comment counts and name length say little about it. Topic 7.1, lesson “7.1 · Code quality: cohesion, coupling, duplication and smells”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why do code reviews and pairing improve code quality beyond catching bugs?

options.text: They reduce the code to fewer lines each time
They let managers rate each developer's skill
They spread shared standards and design sense
They replace the need for automated tests

questions.explanation: Reviews and pairing align the team on conventions and design choices and spread knowledge of the code, which supports collective ownership. They complement automated tests. Topic 7.1, lesson “7.1 · Code quality: cohesion, coupling, duplication and smells”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which SOLID principle says high-level and low-level modules should both rely on abstractions?

options.text: Dependency inversion
Open-closed
Single responsibility
Interface segregation

questions.explanation: Dependency inversion says both high- and low-level modules depend on abstractions, which in C# usually means constructor-injected interfaces. It is what makes swapping implementations easy. Topic 7.2, lesson “7.2 · SOLID and other design principles”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A C# class implements INotifier but throws NotImplementedException for SendSms. Which principle is most likely broken?

options.text: Interface segregation
Single responsibility
Open-closed
Dependency inversion

questions.explanation: A fat interface forces implementers to support methods they do not need. Splitting it into smaller, focused interfaces lets each class implement only what it does. Topic 7.2, lesson “7.2 · SOLID and other design principles”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does the open-closed principle reduce risk?

options.text: All code is closed to other teams for review
New behaviour is added without editing tested code
Classes can never be changed once they are released
Open code can be copied freely between projects

questions.explanation: When new behaviour arrives as a new class behind an existing abstraction, the tested code is untouched, so regressions are less likely. It does not forbid fixing or refactoring code. Topic 7.2, lesson “7.2 · SOLID and other design principles”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A Square class inherits from Rectangle, and setting its width also changes its height, which breaks callers. Which principle is violated?

options.text: Liskov substitution
Interface segregation
Open-closed
Single responsibility

questions.explanation: Liskov substitution says a subtype must work wherever its base type is expected. Callers of Rectangle assume width and height are independent, so Square cannot stand in for it. Topic 7.2, lesson “7.2 · SOLID and other design principles”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An InvoiceService both calculates totals and formats PDF output. Which change best applies the single responsibility principle?

options.text: Move the PDF rendering into its own class
Add comments to separate the two concerns
Make all the methods static for simplicity
Rename the class to InvoiceAndPdfService

questions.explanation: Totals and PDF layout change for different reasons, so they belong in different classes. Renaming or commenting leaves two reasons to change in one place. Topic 7.2, lesson “7.2 · SOLID and other design principles”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does dependency inversion support testing in C#?

options.text: It removes the need for constructors in classes
It lets tests run without compiling the code
Code relies on interfaces, so tests pass fakes
It makes all classes static and easy to call

questions.explanation: When a class receives its dependencies as interfaces, a test can supply a stub or mock instead of a real database or service, so it runs fast and deterministically. Static classes would block that. Topic 7.2, lesson “7.2 · SOLID and other design principles”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does YAGNI stand for?

options.text: Your agile group needs iteration
You always get new ideas
You aren't gonna need it
Yet another generic named interface

questions.explanation: YAGNI, from Extreme Programming, warns against building features or flexibility before they are needed, since most speculative work is never used and all of it must be maintained. The other expansions are invented. Topic 7.2, lesson “7.2 · SOLID and other design principles”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A developer adds a plugin system in case customers want plugins one day. Which principle does this break?

options.text: DRY
YAGNI
Liskov substitution
Law of Demeter

questions.explanation: Building for an imagined future need adds complexity now with no guaranteed benefit. YAGNI says to add it when a real need appears, keeping the design simple and easy to extend then. Topic 7.2, lesson “7.2 · SOLID and other design principles”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why can over-applying design principles harm a codebase?

options.text: Principles only apply to code in other languages
Extra abstractions add complexity for no gain
Principles make code run more slowly in production
Principles stop teams from writing any tests

questions.explanation: Interfaces and patterns everywhere make simple code hard to follow. Principles are guides to apply where they solve a real problem, balanced with simple design. Topic 7.2, lesson “7.2 · SOLID and other design principles”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the Law of Demeter advise?

options.text: Talk only to an object's immediate collaborators
Keep each class under one hundred lines of source code
Avoid using interfaces between modules
Name methods after the data they return

questions.explanation: Long chains such as order.Customer.Address.City couple code to the inner structure of other objects. Asking the immediate collaborator for what is needed keeps coupling low. Topic 7.2, lesson “7.2 · SOLID and other design principles”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which pattern provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem?

options.text: Observer
Decorator
Facade
Adapter

questions.explanation: A Facade offers one simple entry point to a set of complex classes. An Adapter converts one interface into another that a client expects. Topic 7.3, lesson “7.3 · Interfaces and design patterns”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team needs to add logging and caching around a repository without changing it, stacking the behaviours. Which pattern fits?

options.text: Adapter
Singleton
Decorator
Factory Method

questions.explanation: Decorators wrap an object behind the same interface and add behaviour, and they can be stacked. In .NET they are often registered through dependency injection around the real repository. Topic 7.3, lesson “7.3 · Interfaces and design patterns”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Several parts of an application must react when an order's status changes. Which pattern fits?

options.text: Facade
Observer
Builder
Adapter

questions.explanation: Observer lets subscribers react to a subject's changes without the subject knowing them in detail; C# events and domain events are common forms. Facade, Builder and Adapter solve other problems. Topic 7.3, lesson “7.3 · Interfaces and design patterns”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What problem does the Factory Method pattern solve?

options.text: Ensuring only one instance of a class exists
Converting one interface into another
Adding behaviour to objects at run time
Letting subclasses pick which class to create

questions.explanation: Factory Method defers creation to subclasses or a method, so client code depends on an abstraction rather than a concrete class. A single instance is Singleton; conversion is Adapter; adding behaviour is Decorator. Topic 7.3, lesson “7.3 · Interfaces and design patterns”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why is the Singleton pattern often discouraged in testable C# code?

options.text: It hides a global dependency tests cannot swap
It always creates too many objects in memory
It is not supported by the .NET runtime
It cannot be used with interfaces in any language

questions.explanation: A static singleton is reached from anywhere, so tests cannot replace it and state leaks between tests. A singleton lifetime in the dependency injection container gives one instance without the hidden dependency. Topic 7.3, lesson “7.3 · Interfaces and design patterns”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A C# application must build complex report objects with many optional parts in a readable way. Which pattern fits?

options.text: Observer
Facade
Strategy
Builder

questions.explanation: Builder constructs complex objects step by step with readable, named steps, avoiding constructors with many optional parameters. Observer, Facade and Strategy address other needs. Topic 7.3, lesson “7.3 · Interfaces and design patterns”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the advice 'program to an interface' mean?

options.text: Implement each interface method in one class
Write the user interface before the business logic
Avoid classes and use static methods throughout
Depend on what a type does, not its concrete class

questions.explanation: Depending on abstractions lets implementations change or be substituted, for example in tests, without changing the code that uses them. It has nothing to do with user interfaces. Topic 7.3, lesson “7.3 · Interfaces and design patterns”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which pattern lets a text editor undo user actions by storing each action as an object?

options.text: Singleton
Command
Adapter
Facade

questions.explanation: Command turns a request into an object with Execute and often Undo methods, so actions can be queued, logged and reversed. Adapter, Facade and Singleton cannot do that. Topic 7.3, lesson “7.3 · Interfaces and design patterns”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: When should a team introduce a design pattern?

options.text: When the problem it solves is actually present
When a pattern has not been used for a while
Before any code is written, to be safe
Whenever a new class is added to the codebase

questions.explanation: Patterns are named solutions to recurring problems; applied without the problem, they add indirection for no benefit. Refactoring towards a pattern when the need appears is common. Topic 7.3, lesson “7.3 · Interfaces and design patterns”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and lets subclasses fill in some steps?

options.text: Observer
Template Method
Strategy
Decorator

questions.explanation: Template Method fixes the order of steps in a base class and lets subclasses override specific steps. Strategy swaps the whole algorithm through composition instead of inheritance. Topic 7.3, lesson “7.3 · Interfaces and design patterns”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How do interfaces help teams work in parallel?

options.text: Teams agree the contract and build both sides
Interfaces let one team write all the code alone
Interfaces make every class public to other teams
Interfaces remove the need for integration tests

questions.explanation: An agreed interface lets one team build the provider and another the consumer, each testing against the contract with doubles. Integration tests still confirm the two fit. Topic 7.3, lesson “7.3 · Interfaces and design patterns”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is Test-Driven Development?

options.text: Writing tests for the code once a feature has been completed
Testing through the user interface
Having testers drive the iteration plan
Building and running a test before the code it checks

questions.explanation: TDD is a philosophy and practice of building and running tests before implementing the code or component. Writing tests afterwards checks the code but does not shape its design. Topic 8.1, lesson “8.1 · The TDD cycle”. Source: SAFe · Test-Driven Development; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: A developer at Radley Pay has written a new test and seen it fail. What is the next step in the TDD cycle?

options.text: Write three more tests
Write the complete implementation along with its edge cases
Write the simplest code that makes the test pass
Refactor the surrounding module

questions.explanation: After red comes green: the smallest change that passes the test. Refactoring follows once the test passes, and writing the complete implementation at once skips the feedback the cycle is for. Topic 8.1, lesson “8.1 · The TDD cycle”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does a developer watch a new test fail before writing the code?

options.text: To slow the pace of change
To record a baseline for the team's velocity in the tool
To give the reviewer evidence of effort
To confirm the test can detect the missing behaviour

questions.explanation: A test that passes before the code exists is not testing what the developer thinks, so the failing run validates the test itself. It has nothing to do with velocity. Topic 8.1, lesson “8.1 · The TDD cycle”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is refactoring?

options.text: Removing tests that fail
Fixing defects reported by customers
Rewriting a component so that it supports a new feature for users
Improving internal structure without changing external behaviour

questions.explanation: Refactoring improves the internal structure or operation of code or a component without changing its external behaviour. Adding a feature changes behaviour, so it is a separate step. Topic 8.3, lesson “8.3 · Refactoring safely”. Source: SAFe · Refactoring; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: A team at Selwyn Health needs a larger refactoring that will take several days. How does SAFe treat this work?

options.text: As a task outside the backlog
As hidden effort spread across the other stories in the plan
As an enabler story that is estimated and accepted
As work for the IP iteration alone

questions.explanation: The refactoring article says refactors are a type of enabler story and must be estimable, verifiable and valuable like any story, accepted by the product owner. Hiding the effort makes the plan and the velocity untrue. Topic 8.3, lesson “8.3 · Refactoring safely”. Source: SAFe · Refactoring.

questions.prompt: New behaviour is needed in a tangled class at Tolland Bank. Which order of work is safest?

options.text: Add the behaviour in a copy of the class
Rewrite the class and its tests together in one large change
Add the behaviour first, then tidy the class if time remains
Refactor under passing tests, then add the behaviour test-first

questions.explanation: Changing structure and behaviour in separate steps keeps each one safe: first make the change easy under green tests, then make the change. Tidying if time remains usually means the tidying never happens. Topic 8.3, lesson “8.3 · Refactoring safely”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A unit test at Upton Retail calls a real payment gateway and fails when the network is slow. Which kind of test double supplies a canned reply?

options.text: A production clone
A stub
A load generator
A spy that records calls

questions.explanation: A stub returns prepared answers so the unit can be tested in isolation and at speed. A spy also stands in for a dependency, but its purpose is to record how it was called. Topic 8.2, lesson “8.2 · Test doubles and unit test design”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the TDD cycle in order.

options.text: Write a small test for the next behaviour
Refactor with all tests passing
Run it and see it fail
Write the simplest code that passes

questions.explanation: The cycle is red, green, refactor: a failing test, the simplest passing code, then a clean-up under green tests. Refactoring comes last because the passing tests are what make it safe. Topic 8.1, lesson “8.1 · The TDD cycle”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What are the three steps of the TDD cycle?

options.text: Write, run, deploy
Plan, code, test
Red, green, refactor
Design, build, review

questions.explanation: Write a failing test (red), write the simplest code to pass it (green), then improve the design with all tests passing (refactor). The cycle repeats in small steps. Topic 8.1, lesson “8.1 · The TDD cycle”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: After making a test pass with simple code, what should a developer do next in TDD?

options.text: Write the next feature without tests
Refactor with all tests kept green
Commit and skip any further changes
Delete the test now that it passes

questions.explanation: The refactor step cleans up duplication and naming while the tests protect behaviour. Skipping it accumulates debt cycle by cycle. Topic 8.1, lesson “8.1 · The TDD cycle”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does TDD favour very small steps?

options.text: Small steps let developers skip refactoring
Large steps make tests run more slowly each time
Small steps are required by the xUnit framework
A failure points straight to the last change

questions.explanation: When each step is tiny, a failing test identifies the cause at once, so debugging time almost disappears. Small steps also keep the design moving in safe increments. Topic 8.1, lesson “8.1 · The TDD cycle”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which test name best follows good practice in a C# test project?

options.text: Total_IncludesTax_WhenCustomerIsDomestic
CheckEverythingAboutTheInvoiceTotal
TestMethodNumberOneForTheTotal
TotalMethodWorksCorrectlyForAllOfTheCases

questions.explanation: A good test name states the unit, the expected behaviour and the condition, so a failure explains itself. Vague names force a reader to open the test to understand it. Topic 8.1, lesson “8.1 · The TDD cycle”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a mock in unit testing?

options.text: A test that runs against a real service
A double that verifies how it was called
A double that returns fixed answers only
A copy of the production database

questions.explanation: A mock checks interactions, such as whether a method was called with given arguments. A double that just returns fixed answers is a stub. Topic 8.2, lesson “8.2 · Test doubles and unit test design”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A test needs a repository that returns one fixed customer and nothing else. Which double fits?

options.text: A spy on the database
A mock that verifies calls
A real repository
A stub

questions.explanation: A stub supplies canned answers so the code under test can run; nothing about the calls is verified. A real repository would make the test slow and dependent on data. Topic 8.2, lesson “8.2 · Test doubles and unit test design”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a fake in unit testing?

options.text: A copy of production data with the names removed
A test that passes whatever the code does
A working stand-in, such as an in-memory store
A double that records each call made to it

questions.explanation: A fake has real but simplified behaviour, such as an in-memory repository or the EF Core in-memory provider, which suits tests that need state. A double that records calls is a spy. Topic 8.2, lesson “8.2 · Test doubles and unit test design”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why can heavy use of mocks make tests brittle?

options.text: Mocks always hide real defects in the code
Mocks make tests run much more slowly
Mocks cannot be used with interfaces in C#
They couple tests to how code works inside

questions.explanation: Verifying many internal calls ties tests to the implementation, so a refactoring that keeps behaviour still breaks them. Prefer checking outcomes and mock only at real boundaries. Topic 8.2, lesson “8.2 · Test doubles and unit test design”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A unit test for an order service must confirm that an email was requested exactly once. Which double fits?

options.text: A fake in-memory database
A stub that returns a fixed value
A real SMTP server in the test
A mock or spy that records the call

questions.explanation: Checking that an interaction happened, and how often, is what mocks and spies are for. A real SMTP server would make the test slow and unreliable. Topic 8.2, lesson “8.2 · Test doubles and unit test design”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern?

options.text: A test layout: set up, run, then check
A rule for naming classes in a test project
A way to order tests by importance
A process for approving merges into main

questions.explanation: Arrange sets up the objects and data, Act runs the behaviour under test, and Assert checks the result. The shape keeps tests short and readable. Topic 8.2, lesson “8.2 · Test doubles and unit test design”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What makes a unit test trustworthy?

options.text: It covers as many behaviours as it can at once
It depends on the order in which tests run
It is fast, isolated and repeatable
It touches the real database to be realistic

questions.explanation: Good unit tests run in milliseconds, do not depend on each other or on external systems, give the same result every time and check one behaviour, so a failure is meaningful. Real databases and order dependence break that. Topic 8.2, lesson “8.2 · Test doubles and unit test design”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A developer replaces the literal 0.2 with a named constant, VatRate. What is the main gain?

options.text: The compiler can now skip some of its type checks
The tests for the class no longer need to run
The program runs noticeably faster at run time
The meaning is clear and changes are made once

questions.explanation: Replacing a magic number with a named constant documents intent and removes duplication, so a rate change is made once. It does not change performance or testing. Topic 8.3, lesson “8.3 · Refactoring safely”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Before refactoring a legacy C# class that has no tests, what should a developer do first?

options.text: Rewrite the class from scratch in one change
Ask a colleague to review the plan only
Refactor carefully and run manual tests afterwards
Add characterization tests first

questions.explanation: Characterization tests record what the code does today, right or wrong, so refactoring can be checked against it. Without them, a refactoring cannot be shown to preserve behaviour. Topic 8.3, lesson “8.3 · Refactoring safely”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should refactoring and adding behaviour be separate steps?

options.text: Behaviour can be added only on Fridays
Each step stays small and easy to trace
Tests run faster when changes are separate
Refactoring is not allowed in the same iteration

questions.explanation: Refactoring should keep all tests green; adding behaviour changes what they expect. Doing one at a time keeps each step verifiable and makes any failure's cause obvious. Topic 8.3, lesson “8.3 · Refactoring safely”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the 'boy scout rule' in code?

options.text: Rewrite a class completely before adding to it
Camp out with the team until the build is green
Leave code you did not write exactly as it is
Leave the code a little cleaner than you found it

questions.explanation: Small, continuous improvements made while working in an area keep debt from growing without big refactoring projects. It suits collective ownership. Topic 8.3, lesson “8.3 · Refactoring safely”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which refactoring is safest in a large C# codebase?

options.text: A manual search-and-replace across all files
An automated rename across all references
Commenting out code that seems unused
Copying the class and editing the copy

questions.explanation: IDE refactorings understand the code's structure, so a rename updates every real reference and nothing else. Text replacement can change unrelated matches and miss others. Topic 8.3, lesson “8.3 · Refactoring safely”. Not checked against a public page.
